elements.element: Customer owns every deliverable created for Customer.
elements.evidence: Unspecified Materials created during the Service performance period default to Type I, but IBM may designate created Materials as Type II, in which IBM or third parties retain ownership.

elements.element: Customer owns all work product created for Customer.
elements.evidence: The clause addresses only defined “Materials” and does not ensure that all work product created for Customer is Customer-owned; created Materials may also be designated Type II.

elements.element: Vendor assigns to Customer its ownership rights in the deliverables and work product created for Customer.
elements.evidence: Section 7(b) states that Customer “will have” rights in Type I Materials but contains no present assignment by IBM, and Section 7(a) permits created Materials to be designated Type II.

elements.element: Vendor retains ownership of its pre-existing intellectual property.
elements.evidence: Materials that pre-exist the Services default to Type II, and Section 7(c) provides that IBM or third parties retain all right, title, and interest in Type II Materials.

elements.element: Customer receives a licence to any Vendor intellectual property embedded in the deliverables.
elements.evidence: The licence covers copies of specified Type II Materials only. It does not expressly cover all IBM intellectual property embedded in Type I or other deliverables, and the absence of embedded IBM IP is not demonstrated.

elements.element: The licence to Vendor intellectual property embedded in the deliverables is perpetual.
elements.evidence: The Type II licence is not stated to be perpetual, and no survival or duration language establishes that it continues indefinitely.

elements.element: The licence to Vendor intellectual property embedded in the deliverables is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: The potentially relevant Type II licence is expressly described as irrevocable.

elements.element: The licence to Vendor intellectual property embedded in the deliverables is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: The Type II licence is “paid-up,” which provides the required no-additional-royalty economic treatment.

elements.element: Customer retains all rights in Customer Data.
elements.evidence: Section 7(e) preserves rights in “Content” and “Customer Components,” but the operative language does not identify those terms as encompassing all Customer Data.

elements.element: No joint ownership is created between Customer and Vendor.
elements.evidence: Type I Materials are allocated entirely to Customer, while Type II Materials are allocated to IBM or third parties; the clause creates no joint ownership between Customer and IBM.

elements.element: Vendor owns its generic tools.
elements.evidence: The clause contains no categorical reservation for generic tools. Newly created generic tools would default to Customer-owned Type I Materials unless IBM designates them Type II.

elements.element: Vendor owns its generic know-how.
elements.evidence: Generic know-how is not expressly reserved to IBM or addressed by the ownership provisions.

elements.element: Customer receives a licence covering all deliverables.
elements.evidence: The express licence covers only specified Type II Materials. Type I Materials are owned by Customer rather than expressly licensed, and other deliverables or work product are not clearly covered.

elements.element: The deliverables licence is perpetual.
elements.evidence: No perpetual duration or equivalent survival language is included.

elements.element: The deliverables licence is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence is expressly irrevocable.

elements.element: The deliverables licence is worldwide.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence is expressly worldwide.

elements.element: The deliverables licence is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence is described as paid-up, providing no-additional-royalty treatment.

elements.element: The deliverables licence permits Customer to use the deliverables.
elements.evidence: The Type II licence expressly permits Customer to “use” the licensed Materials.

elements.element: The deliverables licence permits Customer to modify the deliverables.
elements.evidence: No modification, adaptation, or derivative-work right is granted for Type II Materials.

elements.element: The deliverables licence permits Customer to sublicense the deliverables.
elements.evidence: No sublicensing right is granted. The distribution right is limited to Customer’s Enterprise and does not authorize downstream licensing.

elements.element: The deliverables licence permits exploitation for Customer’s business.
elements.evidence: Use and distribution are limited to Customer’s Enterprise only, which is narrower than the requested business-use scope and does not support the required modification and sublicensing activities.

result.reason: The redline improves the default ownership allocation and adds a reservation for Content and Customer Components, but IBM can still designate created Materials as Type II, there is no operative assignment, and embedded IBM IP is not given a perpetual licence. The fallback also fails because the licence is not perpetual and lacks modification, sublicensing, and sufficiently broad business-use rights. The changes are related to the stated IP objective and do not introduce a clear contradiction, but they do not complete either position and retain drafting defects such as the dangling “Customer grants to IBM:” language.
